name: Files.readAllBytes()
desc: Reads the whole file as raw bytes. The right call for an image, a zip, or a PDF, where a charset would corrupt the content.
body: The file must exist; a missing path throws `NoSuchFileException`. Loading everything is fine for a photo and wrong for a large archive, where `Files.newInputStream` keeps memory flat. When the file does not fit, the failure is `OutOfMemoryError`, not `IOException`, so a catch block for `IOException` will not see it.

name: Files.write() with byte[]
desc: Writes a byte array to a file. With no options it creates the file or replaces the existing content.
body: The default options are `CREATE`, `TRUNCATE_EXISTING`, `WRITE`, so the call replaces old content. Pass `StandardOpenOption.APPEND` to add bytes at the end, and remember that `APPEND` alone fails on a missing file, so pair it with `CREATE`. The text overloads of `Files.write` encode characters; this one does not touch a charset.

name: Files.copy()
desc: Copies a file's content to another path. Without REPLACE_EXISTING it fails when the target already exists.
body: Without the option the call throws `FileAlreadyExistsException`. Content is copied, attributes are not; add `StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES` when timestamps matter. Copying a directory creates an empty directory at the target and does not recurse. The parent of the target must exist, because `Files.copy` does not create it.

name: Files.move()
desc: Moves or renames a file. On the same filesystem it is a rename, and the bytes are not rewritten.
body: `StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE` asks for a single step that either happens or does not; it throws `AtomicMoveNotSupportedException` when the filesystem cannot promise that. Across disks the move is a copy followed by a delete, so it costs time proportional to the file size and is not atomic. Moving a non-empty directory fails. `Path.resolveSibling` is the shortest way to rename in place.

name: Files.deleteIfExists()
desc: Deletes a file or an empty directory and reports whether something was removed. A missing path is not an error.
body: Use this in cleanup code, where the file may already be gone. `Files.delete` is the strict version: it throws `NoSuchFileException` for a missing path and `DirectoryNotEmptyException` for a folder that still holds files. Neither call uses a recycle bin, so a wrong path is gone for good.

name: Files.walk()
desc: Returns a Stream of paths under a directory, to a chosen depth. The stream holds a directory handle and must be closed.
body: The two argument form takes a maximum depth: 0 is the root alone, 1 adds its children. The walk does not follow symbolic links unless you pass `FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS`, which is what stops a link loop from running forever. `sorted()` pulls every path into memory before it emits one, so it belongs on a tree you expect to fit. Collect inside the `try` and work with the list after it; a lazily consumed stream that escapes its block is a file handle leak.

name: Delete a directory tree
desc: Removes every file under a folder and then the folder itself. Deleting children first is what makes each step legal.
body: Reverse path order puts `a/b/x.txt` before `a/b` and `a` before `scratch`, so `Files.delete` never sees a non-empty directory. A locked file on Windows produces an `IOException` on that path only, which is why the try sits inside the loop. `Files.walk` offers no force delete; there is no one call that removes a non-empty tree.

name: Files.createTempFile()
desc: Creates a uniquely named empty file in the given directory. The name is generated, so two runs cannot collide.
body: Pass no directory and the file lands in `java.io.tmpdir`, which is a different filesystem on many machines and turns the later move into a copy. The file is not deleted when the JVM exits; `deleteOnExit` exists on `File` but it only runs on a normal shutdown and keeps a reference until then. Create it next to the target and clean it in a `finally`.

name: Files.readAttributes()
desc: Returns type, size, and timestamps for one path in a single call, instead of four separate probes.
body: For a directory, `size()` is a filesystem specific number and not the total of its contents. The attributes object says what the entry is; it does not carry Unix permission bits. Those need `PosixFileAttributes` and a `PosixFilePermission` set, which is a different call and is not portable to Windows. `Files.readAttributes` follows symbolic links by default; `LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS` describes the link itself.

name: Files.mismatch()
desc: Returns the index of the first differing byte, or -1 when two files have identical content. Java 12 and later.
body: Both files must exist, otherwise the call throws `NoSuchFileException`. When one file is a prefix of the other, the shorter length is returned, so a truncated copy is reported at the point where it ends. The comparison reads in chunks and never holds either file in memory, which makes it safe for two large files.

name: Files.size()
desc: Returns the length of a file in bytes. For a directory the number is filesystem specific and means nothing useful.
body: The count is bytes, not characters. In UTF-8 an accented letter or an emoji takes more than one byte, so a limit written in characters will not match a limit written in bytes. A missing file throws `NoSuchFileException`; guard with `Files.exists` when the path is optional. To measure a folder, sum the sizes of the files under it.
